scenes.title: Turn a five-square shape
scenes.narration: A shape has a row of four unit squares and one extra square attached underneath the left end. How many unit squares are in it after a quarter turn? Picture the solid piece turning without coming apart.

scenes.title: Follow the five cells
scenes.narration: The top row has four cells. The extra cell shares an edge but is a different square. A quarter turn moves each cell to one new position. It preserves the five squares and the same area.

scenes.title: Two corners leave the board
scenes.narration: A five by three board has two corner cells removed. Can you tile what remains using pieces of exactly three unit squares? Pieces may be turned. They may not overlap, and each cell must be covered.

scenes.title: Count what the tiles can cover
scenes.narration: The original board has fifteen cells, and removing the corners leaves thirteen. Every piece covers exactly three squares. An exact cover would require thirteen to be divisible by three. There would be leftover cells even before any shape restrictions were checked. The tiling is impossible.

scenes.title: Begin at the left edge
scenes.narration: Tile a two-row board of width nine using dominoes. Exactly three dominoes must stand vertically and cover both rows of their column. How many tilings work? A horizontal domino in the leftmost uncovered column creates a forced placement beside it.

scenes.title: Build with two block types
scenes.narration: Look at the leftmost column still uncovered. A vertical domino fills one column. If you put a horizontal domino there, the other cell of the column must start another horizontal domino. The three vertical dominoes use three columns. After that, six columns are covered by three pairs of horizontal dominoes. Choose the three positions occupied by the vertical blocks among the six blocks. The other positions are occupied by horizontal pairs.

scenes.title: Count every tiling once
scenes.narration: The number of choices is twenty. Each sequence of these two block types gives a legal tiling when expanded from the left. A finished tiling determines its block sequence from the leftmost uncovered column on each step. That gives only one count per tiling.
